articles.title: Nvidia’s AI chips are no longer welcome in China
articles.summary: Chinese tech companies cannot buy NVIDIA’s RTX Pro 6000D chips any more, the Financial Times reported.
articles.body: Alibaba, ByteDance, and other Chinese technology companies are barred from purchasing Nvidia’s latest AI chips custom-made for China, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday. The Cyberspace Administration of China banned buying and testing the RTX Pro 6000D chips, despite companies having ordered thousands of the chips in the months since their introduction in July, according to three unnamed people with knowledge of the matter and who spoke to the FT. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he was “disappointed” by news of the ban during a press conference with reporters in London, where he is set to join President Donald Trump at a state dinner on Wednesday night. In August, Nvidia worked with Trump to broker a deal allowing the sale of H20 chips to China in return for a 15 percent cut of the profit. “We probably contributed more to the China market than most countries have. And I’m disappointed with what I see,” Huang said to reporters during the press conference. “But they have larger agendas to work out between China and the United States, and I’m understanding of that.” Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson went further, saying that China is trying to become a “peer-to-peer adversary” of the US during an interview with CNBC’s “Squawk Box” on Wednesday. “They have no regard whatsoever for U.S. trademark law or any of the other provisions that make for fair trade agreements,” Johnson said. “It is not the fault of the United States that there are these strained relations. It is the fault of China.” China has been making moves to build up its own chip manufacturing capability after years of tit-for-tat export controls by the US to limit the sale of AI chips to China, and China limiting the sale of chip materials to the US. China has been using less powerful chips tailor-made for the country by Nvidia.

articles.title: Honey Ordóñez, la modelo colombiana que brillará en Victoria's Secret Fashion Show
articles.summary: La industria de la moda internacional vuelve a poner sus ojos en el talento colombiano. A sus 20 años, la modelo colombo-nicaragüense Honey Ordóñez se prepara para hacer historia al convertirse en la segunda mujer colombiana en desfilar en el icónico Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, consolidando el lugar del país en uno de los escenarios más influyentes del modelaje global.
articles.body: La industria de la moda internacional vuelve a poner sus ojos en el talento colombiano. A sus 20 años, la modelo colombo-nicaragüense Honey Ordóñez se prepara para hacer historia al convertirse en la segunda mujer colombiana en desfilar en el icónico Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show, consolidando el lugar del país en uno de los escenarios más influyentes del modelaje global. Nacida en la isla de San Andrés y con raíces nicaragüenses por parte de su madre, Ordóñez ha tenido que recorrer un camino de constancia y perseverancia para alcanzar este hito. Tras haberse presentado a dos castings previos sin éxito, la tercera fue la vencida para la joven modelo, quien obtuvo su codiciado cupo para la esperada edición del desfile en Los Ángeles, California. Con un emotivo mensaje compartido en sus redes sociales, acompañado de las banderas de Colombia y Nicaragua y los característicos emojis de alas de ángel, la modelo expresó su incredulidad y emoción: “¡GUAU, todavía lo estoy asimilando! No podría estar más emocionada de ser parte del legendario Victoria's Secret Show... ¡Vamos con toda! Mi yo de 8 años no me lo creería”. Aunque este debut marca un punto álgido en su carrera, el nombre de Honey Ordóñez no es desconocido en las grandes ligas de la moda. Su talento y versatilidad la han llevado a colaborar con marcas de lujo y casas editoriales de gran prestigio a nivel mundial: Consolidación en pasarelas de lujo: Ha desfilado para firmas de la talla de Dior (bajo la dirección creativa de Maria Grazia Chiuri), además de participar en las semanas de la moda de París y Milán para marcas como JW Anderson. Campañas globales y editoriales: Protagonizó una campaña global para Dior y ha trabajado con marcas reconocidas como Benetton, Puma, Ralph Lauren y Bally. Asimismo, su rostro ha aparecido en las páginas de publicaciones tan importantes como Vogue Latinoamérica, TIME y Le Magazine du Monde. La llegada de Honey Ordóñez a esta prestigiosa pasarela sigue los pasos de la también colombiana Valentina Castro, quien abrió la puerta para el país en el radar de la marca estadounidense. Con su participación, Ordóñez no solo representa la diversidad geográfica y cultural del Caribe colombiano desde San Andrés, sino que ratifica que el talento de las nuevas generaciones del país continúa rompiendo fronteras y conquistando los escenarios más exigentes de la moda internacional.

images.caption: Honey Ordóñez es la nueva colombiana en el Victoria's Secret Fashion Show. Instagram

articles.title: CoreWeave’s Business Is Sound Despite Debt Fears, JPMorgan Says
articles.summary: Investor concerns over CoreWeave Inc.’s mounting debt and rapid cash burn are likely overdone, analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co. said, given that rapid expans...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Investor concerns over CoreWeave Inc.'s mounting debt and rapid cash burn are likely overdone, analysts at JPMorgan Chase & Co. said, given that rapid expansion is driving its financing needs rather than weak project economics.

Shares of the AI computing provider plunged about 20% last week as rising bond yields fueled concerns over its debt-funded expansion, contributing to a market-wide selloff. A Gartner forecast questioning whether AI revenue would be sufficient to support healthy returns on the industry's massive infrastructure investments exacerbated investor worries.

But CoreWeave's business model remains sound, JPMorgan equity analysts including Samik Chatterjee wrote in a Friday note, pointing to strong demand for computing power and long-term take-or-pay contracts that secure customers before new capacity comes online.

The analysts estimate that a typical five-year contract generates an unlevered internal rate of return in the mid-teens, exceeding the company's estimated blended cost of capital of 9% to 11%.

"Beyond the sound economics on a project for a typical 5-year contract agreement, there is an additional monetization lever in recontracting GPUs beyond the 5-year duration," the analysts added.

The company's contract economics also provide a cushion against debt risks. In a conservative scenario, capital spending represents about 51% of a five-year contract's value, with roughly 80% financed through asset-level debt, the bank said. After repaying that debt, CoreWeave could retain cash equal to about 16% of the contract value, enough to cover roughly five years of data center obligations even without renewing the contract.

That said, CoreWeave's aggressive expansion is expected to keep pressure on cash flow in the near term. The bank estimates that each gigawatt of fully operational capacity could generate $10 billion to $15 billion in annual revenue. Meanwhile, adding a gigawatt requires more than $35 billion in upfront capital spending.

"The cash burn is not a function of unfavorable economics per project but more of the capacity being ramped each year relative to the installed active capacity at this time," the analysts wrote.

articles.title: Morgan Stanley’s favorite AI stock is 92% exposed to the $1.6 trillion build-out it’s bullish on
articles.summary: The bank calls Nvidia the best risk/reward in AI. Its own report lays out what happens to suppliers when a capital cycle turns.
articles.body:
By Morgan Stanley's count, 91.7% of Nvidia's 2027 revenue is exposed to one thing: AI infrastructure demand. No company on the bank's list scores higher. Not Vertiv , at 90%. Not Broadcom , at 81%.

The same report, published Oct. 15, calls Nvidia the best risk/reward in the sector.

The bull case for the world's most valuable company and the bull case for the build-out are now essentially the same case, and Morgan Stanley's North America Insight, led by Nicholas Lentini, makes both. The note, titled Following AI's $1.6 Trillion Money Trail: Mapping the Revenue Generated by the Capex Boom, includes a section that runs under the heading "We Are Bullish This Spend." The 65-page note also spends a good part of its length explaining how the spending could break.

Nvidia's defenders would say that exposure describes the company. Its data center business has supplied the large majority of its revenue for years, but the report adds a closer look on how few buyers that exposure runs through.

The firm estimates hyperscalers and AI cloud providers will spend $1.58 trillion in 2027, up roughly 60% from about $980 billion this year, and will spend $1.8 trillion in 2028. About $195 billion of the 2027 figure is data center leases, which never show up as capital spending on a cash flow statement. The report calls leases "synthetic capex." Hyperscalers have disclosed more than $1.1 trillion in lease commitments that haven't started yet.

About $1 trillion of the 2027 spending lands as S&P 500 revenue, by Morgan Stanley's estimate. Nearly $700 billion of it goes to Nvidia. Revenue from hyperscaler and neocloud customers makes up 5% of total S&P 500 revenue in 2027 but drives about 25% of the index's revenue growth.

Nvidia's own customer list is even narrower. In the bank's model, SpaceX and Amazon Web Services together account for about 54% of Nvidia's hyperscaler revenue in 2027 and 72% of its growth.

Morgan Stanley's argument is that Nvidia is cheap for what it is. The stock trades at 15 times fiscal 2028 earnings, and the bank says multiple expansion "is also not required for the stock to work as numbers continue to go higher." It expects the spending to earn 25% to 50% on invested capital. It also argues Wall Street has underestimated compute cycles by 38%, on average, based on four past cycles: PCs, the internet, mobile, and cloud.

The bank even says its own Nvidia numbers may be low. It calls its SpaceX and Amazon estimates conservative, creating "a low bar for remaining hyperscalers." Its model has Nvidia's share of the other hyperscalers' spending slipping from 18% in 2026 to 16% in 2027. Nvidia expects to gain share.

articles.title: Robot Brains For 75 Cents/Hour? Former Nvidia Researchers Raise $90 Million
articles.summary: Want to make your dumb robot smart? $3 an hour is all it costs. Or 75 cents, if you’re okay with a slightly less capable physical AI model.
articles.body:
Want to make your dumb robot smart? $3 an hour is all it costs. Or 75 cents, if you're okay with a slightly less capable physical AI model. Dream Labs, a San Francisco startup founded this year by former leaders of Nvidia's GR00T robotics research team, announced a $90 million seed round today. Dream Labs also launched the Dream API, which it says is the first publicly available API for a robot foundation model.

It's kind of magic: send the API your robot's camera feed plus some plain-English instructions, and it essentially operates your robot … even if it has never seen that particular model before. The team behind the startup says this is the missing link in physical AI.

"The hardware is ready. What's been missing is a brain any robot can use," CEO and co-founder Joel Jang said in a statement. "When you get into a rental car, you don't relearn how to drive. You find the controls and your past driving experience does the rest. Dream-1 approaches a new robot the same way, so a new robot can do useful work in minutes, not months."

The model behind it is called Dream-1. Dream-1 is trained on video of people doing everyday tasks (just like Figure with Index or Neura Robotics in Germany). The model predicts what will happen next in a scene, then works out what the robot should do about it. Because it learns from human video rather than from one specific machine with one specific set of instruction software, Dream Labs says the skills transfer across hardware.

And they've got a big claim: out of the box, Dream-1 can control any robot with two arms and parallel grippers. Essentially instantly, or zero-shot, as roboticists say.

Cross-embodiment transfer – teaching robot B to do what robot A is already doing – is one of the hardest problems in robotics. Almost every robot on the planet is specifically trained for its specific body and its specific task. What one machine learns rarely transfers to another, which has slightly different arms, hands, motors, geometry, friction, and more. There are about 5 million industrial robots working in factories globally, according to Dream Labs, and nearly all of them are programmed for a single task.

Six months ago, Jang says, adapting the team's model to a new robot took 30 minutes of data from that robot. Before that, getting anything working could take 100,000 hours.

"That was six months ago. Now we just need the robot."

The trick is treating robot control as a video problem. "If the AI model can predict a video of a robot doing it, then it can do it," Jang says. "So now control becomes a video prediction problem."

articles.title: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be hardest to stop
articles.summary: The time to prepare for "gradual disempowerment" is now, according to researchers. One calls it "a civilization-scale problem."
articles.body:
It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.

But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."

It's not just a threat to jobs . They warn that allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.

One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.

And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.

"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.

Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks , which could be accelerated by capable AI.

"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."

What is "gradual disempowerment" and how could AI cause it?

The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.

At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.

AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems , doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture .

We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.

It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.

To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.

But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.

But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.

Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.

Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.

The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?

With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.

"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.

"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"

It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military , for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.

If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle , its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.

"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.

States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?

"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.

Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.

If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.

"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.

"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."

How does humanity avoid gradual disempowerment?

Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.

Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can bring to economic, cultural and state functions."

"We can't be in the situation where we are competing with the machines," said Kulveit. "Because if we are just competing with the machines, we will probably lose."

The gradual disempowerment authors believe stopping our disempowerment may be a heavy lift for humanity, since it involves complex systems that feed into each other — government, culture, and the economy.

"This may be a bigger challenge than merely preventing AI systems from pursuing overtly harmful goals," they write.

One first step in slowing disempowerment is keeping indicators of how much work is being ceded to AI, and of what kind of specific jobs AI systems are capable of handling. If thousands of workers are being displaced by AI in, say, call center jobs , it helps to know that in granular detail.

But measurement isn't enough without action, Mitchell said. She argues that removing humans from the loop in AI processes both worsens oversight and degrades the skills of the human overseer. Therefore, companies and leadership in all fields must take proactive steps to keep humans engaged.

"This general practice within tech is we want our systems to be frictionless," said Mitchell, referring to the idea that everything should move fast and without obstacles. "There's this sense that the less friction the better, but there's been a push within the more ethical AI community that strategic friction can be good because it can draw people's attention to critical issues that otherwise they might overlook."

Mitchell argues that strategic friction — keeping humans in the work loop at predetermined steps — can be done both by developers of AI, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic and Google, and by companies and organizations that deploy AI. Thoughtful and purposeful design of AI can benefit society as a whole, and the individuals who use it.

Kulveit agrees that AI should be thoughtfully designed to add value to humans, not necessarily replace our every task.

"You want to carve out places where we agree that we will not allow competitive pressures to remove humans from the loop," he said. "It would be nice if the companies train the AIs to be more complementary to humans. Currently, the AIs are implicitly trained to be a replacement for humans. But you can imagine training the AIs so they are better at explaining to us what's happening."

Kulveit is describing AI that doesn't just spew out the answers to whatever question you ask it, at the very least in sectors where it is critical to include human expertise and decision-making, like war. Quick and easy answers can be helpful, but they can also make you dependent and credulous, believing anything the chatbot tells you, whether right or wrong .

But AI can be more than that. It can help you not just by doing the work for you, but by educating you along the way. That way the human worker continues to learn while using AI as a partner, not a substitute.

"There has been such a singular focus on capability or functionality of these systems to the detriment of people, to the detriment of users," said Mitchell. "If your only goal is to get a high score on a benchmark, then you are not going to be taking into account cognitive support design. But if your goal is to make a system that works really well for people — like if the race is for a utility as opposed to benchmark score — then you end up designing fundamentally different systems."

If gradual disempowerment really is a large-scale risk, compared to more talked-about doom scenarios — like AI helping to design bioweapons or chemical weapons — it may suffer from a relative lack of vividness.

"We know what it means for a robot to take over the world. We know what it means for countries to nuke each other," said Chooi. "AI taking over the world is very legible in the human consciousness. But gradual disempowerment? No one has made a movie about gradual disempowerment."

But to Chooi, gradual disempowerment is very easy to picture.

"All the organizations have the incentives to adopt it and phase out humans," he said. "This is a very logical conclusion. It's not very hard to see it."

articles.title: Anthropic makes pledge for public benefit initiative
articles.summary: {beacon} Technology Technology The Big Story Anthropic makes pledge for public benefit initiative The artificial intelligence firm Anthropic announced it will commit 5 percent of its shares to its new public benefit fund as the industry faces heat over its potential impact on society and the labor market. © Patrick Sison, The Associated Press…
articles.body:
Anthropic makes pledge for public benefit initiative

The artificial intelligence firm Anthropic announced it will commit 5 percent of its shares to its new public benefit fund as the industry faces heat over its potential impact on society and the labor market.

Anthropic, in a blog post Sunday, said the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will help the company pursue it’s “mission in new ways,” including through large donations to traditional nonprofits or “specific populations.”

The company specifically mentioned AI’s potential impacts on the labor market , writing the technology “may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers.”

“Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed,” the company said, adding the public benefit initiative will “have the versatility to pursue them.”

Stockholders still need to approve the 5 percent commitment, and Anthropic said there is a possibility of setting aside more funds if the company becomes more valuable.

“Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good,” the Claude-maker wrote.

It comes as Anthropic prepares for its initial public offering ( IPO ) as soon as next month.

articles.title: Eric Schmidt’s 1% Anthropic Stake Set to Pay Massive Windfall
articles.summary: Former Google Chief Executive Officer Eric Schmidt owns around 1% of Anthropic PBC thanks to his early investment in the startup, according to people familia...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Former Google Chief Executive Officer Eric Schmidt owns around 1% of Anthropic PBC thanks to his early investment in the startup, according to people familiar with the matter, setting him up for one of the largest individual windfalls from the company's imminent public market debut.

Schmidt invested tens of millions of dollars in Anthropic's Series A fundraising round, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because they weren't authorized to discuss private matters. It's unclear if he has sold any part of his stake since the initial investment.

Schmidt and Anthropic declined to comment.

Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO is set to generate massive windfalls for its employees and investors. The startup's seven co-founders are already worth $8 billion each based on its last funding round, fortunes that propelled them onto the Bloomberg Billionaires Index of the world's 500 richest people.

When Schmidt, 71, made his first bet on Anthropic in 2021, it was valued at $461 million, according to data company Pitchbook. Investors indicated last week that a fair valuation for the company is in the $1.8 trillion to $2 trillion ballpark; the high end of that range would value Anthropic at more than 4,300 times its Series A funding round.

At that value, the Anthropic stake would boost Schmidt's net worth by about one-third to nearly $80 billion, according to Bloomberg's wealth index. Even using Anthropic's most recent valuation of $965 billion, Schmidt adds nearly $10 billion to his existing fortune of $57.5 billion.

Schmidt has become a prolific technology investor over the past decade and a half, across several investment platforms including TomorrowVentures, Innovation Endeavors and his Hillspire family office, which Pitchbook associates with hundreds of different venture capital bets.

His early portfolio focused on consumer internet, software and financial technology, but more recently artificial intelligence has been a major focus, with investments in Mistral AI, Reflection AI and World Labs, as well as Anthropic.

If Anthropic's public stock debuts at a $2 trillion value, his bet on the company would beat Innovation Endeavors' own early bet on Uber Technologies Inc. in 2011. By the time that company went public in 2019, its value had increased about 1,400-fold to $82 billion.

articles.title: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem
articles.summary: Does anyone else hear that ticking sound?
articles.body: CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too. Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else. To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more. “The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying. I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit. CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year. So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue. Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business. Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one. Anyway, some people are buying the dip.

articles.title: Microsoft says AI agents are like insider threats as 'frontier models can't be trusted' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Microsoft wants enterprises to closely watch the agents employees use with systems not controlled by AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic.
articles.body:
Microsoft on Monday introduced new security features designed to protect enterprises from the growing threat of AI agents. The launch comes at Microsoft continues to warn enterprises about the dangers of AI and agents.

Perhaps the most notable addition is Guardian Agents , a new feature intended to monitor the AI agents a company uses. Guardian Agents is part of Project Perception, a product introduced in June.

Project Perception was Microsoft’s answer to powerful hacking models like Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable and OpenAI’s security vulnerability scanning system Daybreak. Project Perception originally launched three classes of agents: a “red team” that acted like hackers and attacked, a “blue team” that detected the red team and assessed the vulnerabilities they found, and a “green team” tasked with fixing them.

The product was designed around the assumption that AI hackers would come from outside the company. But lately, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has been warning that the AI enemy may be the very agents enterprises have deployed and are paying for, much like a rogue human employee, otherwise known as an “insider threat.”

Earlier this month, in his private blog , Nadella warned that it’s time to stop trusting AI model providers, even if they offer assurances of safety and security with their agentic products. He wants enterprises to implement separate systems, not controlled by the AI labs, to watch and control the agents that those AI labs’ products launch.

“We are deploying these complex agentic systems and models, with access to our most sensitive data and giving them the ability to take mission-critical actions on our behalf!” he wrote. “We simply can’t outsource responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf. A model provider’s assurances do not relieve us of that responsibility. … In other words, we need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

When announcing Guardian Agents, Microsoft’s security business chief Hayete Gallot was even more straightforward.

“Unfortunately, frontier models, regardless of their origin, cannot be trusted,” she wrote, adding that this isn’t because they are malicious or easily hacked, but because they are unpredictable. They have been trained to achieve tasks, not follow “organizational norms or judgment.”

On top of that, they are often given the keys to the kingdom, with access to data and tools that could do serious harm.

Microsoft’s solution is both surprising and self-serving. The surprising side is that Microsoft is famously close to OpenAI and Anthropic, having invested in both. OpenAI is also one of its biggest cloud customers, and Microsoft has its own AI lab developing models. So, Microsoft is sowing distrust against some of its own business interests.

The self-serving side is that Microsoft wants enterprises to buy agent security products from it, the cloud provider, rather than from Anthropic and OpenAI. But conflicting interests aside, its logic is sound. The software that monitors agent behavior should be separate from the suppliers of agents, just as auditors should be independent of the organizations they audit.

Or as Nadella puts it: “We need to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it.”

Microsoft is now seizing that business opportunity in a variety of ways. In addition to Guardian Agents, it has added an agent detection feature to its Microsoft Defender product that can find up to 60 types of agents that employees bring into the workplace, including Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw. It has also added features that limit agents’ access to data and systems, and dynamically adjust their agent permissions based on the task. That includes requiring human approval if an agent appears to be making risky decisions.

This idea of agents as untrustworthy insiders is taking hold across the broader industry, too.

Microsoft was an inaugural member of Nvidia’s new Open Agent Safety Platform, which garnered the support of more than 100 other tech companies. The platform isolates agents in secure environments and can monitor and stop behavior through hardware, functioning something like a kill switch. This follows Microsoft’s announcement of the new Surface Laptop Ultra PCs built for agents , which run on Nvidia chips and have agent security and controls baked in.

articles.title: Anthropic could be the AI trade’s last tentpole IPO in 2026
articles.summary: Market jitters have forced several AI and fintech companies to reconsider their IPO plans for this year.
articles.body:
Anthropic could be the AI trade's last tentpole IPO in 2026, as postponements of public offerings mount ahead of a looming capital crunch.

Investors earlier in the year salivated at the prospect of successive SpaceX, Anthropic, and OpenAI offerings, but market jitters have forced several fintech and AI-exposed companies to rethink their IPO plans this year.

Anthropic, too, has come under scrutiny, after "more questions than answers emerged around… revenue growth deceleration in September ," an analyst told CNBC, as the startup's revised valuation piles further downward pressure on AI stocks.

Meanwhile, Anthropic is continuing its debt binge but on more exacting terms: Its newest borrowing from Blackstone is expected to charge more than 10% interest , the Financial Times reported.

articles.title: Embedded AI evaluators won't be an easy solution, Hugging Face's policy chief says | TechCrunch
articles.summary: AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure
articles.body:
AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking — the supposedly neutral and accurate system of evaluations that are designed to measure whether one AI product is better than another.

However, the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, said Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, during a discussion at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. Testing needs to come together into a more consistent science if the industry is to rely on them in the future.

With that in mind, can we trust the current tests that are being released?

“Trust is such a weighted term,” said Solaiman. “In terms of whether we can trust results, one big part [of that] is can you reproduce the results of an evaluation? Do you have the level of access that you need to the model itself — this is where open weights come in in a big way,” she added.

Reproducibility in model evaluations has long remained one of the stickier aspects of benchmarking — and remains a topic of significant debate in the industry.

Outside of an individual test’s validity, there’s also the added question of how that test compares to other evaluations.

“They are an evolving science — where we don’t know how to meaningfully compare them to each other,” Solaiman said.

“They start to get ineffective relatively quickly, and we don’t have as much of a thriving ecosystem as we need,” she added. “There’s this hunger for an embedded evaluator ecosystem now, but the qualifications that determine who is an effective evaluator across what tasks need a lot more standardization.”

The idea of embedded evaluators — in which supposedly “neutral” third-party observers are placed inside AI organizations — has been popularized over the last several months, as AI labs grapple with a rash of safety incidents that have spurred concerns over the potential harms of their technology. Hugging Face was famously the target of one of those incidents.

Instead of active government regulation to identify and mitigate model safety concerns, labs have pushed for the third-party solution. However, doubts remain over how neutral or effective those evaluators will actually be. Anthropic’s decision to hire Accenture as its first evaluator spurred a good amount of backlash, with some critics mocking the idea that the consulting firm was qualified to do the task at hand.

Evaluations are now moving from merely a test of the model itself to a test of the entire system around the model — including the harness and agent. The harness — or the tool the user is using to access the model — specifically, has a lot to do with a model’s performance, and a weaker model with a better harness could easily out perform a frontier model, Soleiman shared.

“Agentic evals are really hard and really expensive,” said Solaiman. “We have just more evaluations for models. … We don’t have as many evaluations for harnesses, and we are developing better evaluations for the holistic agent — because that’s what a lot of folks are getting value out of,” she added.

In other words: the evaluation space is a bit of a free-for-all at the moment, and if benchmarking is going to continue to be seen as a useful tool for industry leaders, a more uniform, industry-wide approach — where everyone is on the same page — may be necessary.

articles.title: Nscale and Anthropic are reportedly in talks for yet another $45 billion compute deal | TechCrunch
articles.summary: In August, Nscale and Anthropic announced a $45 billion compute deal. The two companies are reportedly discussing yet another deal of the same magnitude.
articles.body:
A little over a month ago, Anthropic and AI infrastructure provider Nscale announced a $45 billion compute deal . Now, the duo may be about to do it again.

Bloomberg reports that the two companies are said to be on the verge of announcing yet another $45 billion compute deal, citing people familiar with the matter. Those sources cautioned that talks are still under way and that the details could change.

If the deal goes through, it would be the latest in a long string of giant compute deals Anthropic has struck over the past year . TechCrunch reached out to Nscale and Anthropic for more information and will update this story if we hear back.

The massive amount of money being sunk into AI compute deals has spooked a certain segment of investors , who worry that companies are spending too much money for too little profit. Still, Anthropic has pressed on with such partnerships, driven by the belief that it will all pay off in the end.

Both Anthropic and Nscale are also currently pursuing IPOs. Anthropic is still expected to go public this year. Nscale is also seeking to go public, although Bloomberg reported today that the company is experiencing investor pushback over its proposed valuation of $30 billion.

articles.title: Engenharia, dados e IA estão entre as áreas com maior demanda no RJ | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento da Robert Half aponta procura por especialistas em inteligência artificial, engenheiros e lideranças de operações e projetos. Para engenheiros de IA, a faixa salarial estimada chega a R$ 28,2 mil.
articles.summary: Levantamento da Robert Half aponta procura por especialistas em inteligência artificial, engenheiros e lideranças de operações e projetos. Para engenheiros de IA, a faixa salarial
articles.body:
Divulgação — Foto: Engenharia, dados e IA estão entre as áreas com maior demanda no RJ em 2027

Engenharia, dados e inteligência artificial (IA) estão entre as áreas que devem concentrar oportunidades de trabalho no Rio de Janeiro em 2027. Segundo a consultoria Robert Half, empresas também devem buscar profissionais de operações, projetos, desenvolvimento de negócios e Supply Chain.

Para engenheiros especializados em inteligência artificial, a faixa salarial estimada no estado vai de R$ 20,3 mil a R$ 28,2 mil. Os valores fazem parte do Guia Salarial 2027 da consultoria, que reúne estimativas de remuneração para diferentes cargos e níveis profissionais.

Para especialistas em Machine Learning, área ligada ao desenvolvimento de sistemas capazes de aprender com dados, a faixa indicada é de R$ 18,5 mil a R$ 24,25 mil. Já para engenheiros de prompt, profissionais que desenvolvem e aperfeiçoam instruções para sistemas de inteligência artificial, os valores vão de R$ 19,85 mil a R$ 27,15 mil.

Além da tecnologia, o levantamento destaca a demanda por lideranças de Engenharia, Operações e Projetos. A consultoria relaciona o movimento às características da economia fluminense, especialmente aos investimentos em energia, petróleo e gás e infraestrutura.

Veja os salários nas áreas de tecnologia e dados

Na área de IA, o guia apresenta as seguintes faixas salariais para o Rio de Janeiro:

Engenheiro de IA : de R$ 20.300 a R$ 28.200;

Engenheiro de prompt : de R$ 19.850 a R$ 27.150;

Especialista em Machine Learning : de R$ 18.500 a R$ 24.250;

Especialista ou cientista de dados : de R$ 14.450 a R$ 24.150.

As faixas variam conforme a função e o nível de remuneração considerado no levantamento. Para cargos de liderança em tecnologia, a remuneração estimada também pode superar R$ 30 mil. Um gerente de dados tem faixa salarial de R$ 20.050 a R$ 33.500 , enquanto um diretor de tecnologia (CTO) tem valores entre R$ 32.100 e R$ 47.050 .

A demanda prevista para 2027 inclui profissionais que coordenam projetos, processos industriais e operações . Entre as referências salariais do guia, um diretor de Engenharia em empresas de grande porte tem faixa estimada entre R$ 26.600 e R$ 45.850 .

Para diretores de Operações em empresas de grande porte, os valores vão de R$ 28.150 a R$ 48.550 . Já para gerentes de PMO, responsáveis pela estruturação e pelo acompanhamento de projetos, a faixa indicada é de R$ 17.500 a R$ 30.200 .

Engenharia, dados e IA estão entre as áreas com maior demanda no RJ em 2027 — Foto: Divulgação./freepik

Na infraestrutura, os engenheiros de projetos em empresas de grande porte têm remuneração estimada entre R$ 11.350 e R$ 19.650 . Para engenheiros de operação e manutenção (O&M), a faixa vai de R$ 13.650 a R$ 23.700 .

A consultoria apresenta referências distintas para alguns cargos conforme o porte da empresa. Por isso, os valores devem ser interpretados de acordo com a função e a categoria correspondente.

Projetos de energia e petróleo impulsionam demanda

Petróleo e gás, energia e infraestrutura estão entre os segmentos apontados pela Robert Half como aquecidos no estado. Varejo, saúde, educação e tecnologia também aparecem na lista da consultoria.

O levantamento destaca que as contratações no Rio de Janeiro acompanham o desenvolvimento de grandes projetos e as etapas de implantação de novos investimentos. Isso significa que a procura por profissionais pode variar conforme o andamento das iniciativas e a necessidade de cada fase.

“O mercado de trabalho do Rio de Janeiro segue muito ligado a grandes projetos de energia, O&G e infraestrutura, o que faz com que as contratações aconteçam em ondas, acompanhando novos investimentos e fases de implantação”, comenta Vitor Silva, diretor de mercado da Robert Half.

Segundo a consultoria, além de profissionais técnicos, as empresas devem buscar pessoas que combinem conhecimento especializado, visão de negócio e domínio de tecnologia.

A lista de áreas que devem liderar as contratações no estado em 2027 inclui ainda Comercial, Recursos Humanos, Planejamento e Análise Financeira (FP&A) e Controladoria.

Entre os profissionais mais demandados para vagas permanentes, a consultoria destaca especialistas em dados, inteligência artificial e automação, além de profissionais de desenvolvimento de negócios e Supply Chain, área responsável pela cadeia de suprimentos.

O levantamento também aponta oportunidades associadas a projetos temporários ou específicos, como iniciativas ligadas à Reforma Tributária, à renovação de sistemas de gestão empresarial (ERP) e a projetos com retorno sobre o investimento mais claramente definido.

Para a Robert Half, o avanço da tecnologia e a busca por eficiência ampliam a procura por profissionais com perfil híbrido, capazes de combinar competências técnicas e de negócio.

articles.title: É #FAKE imagem de Pantera Cor-de-Rosa nos protestos em Paris | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagens mostram personagem em meio a manifestantes e policiais na capital francesa. Fato ou Fake analisou o material com ferramentas de detecção de IA.
articles.summary: Imagens mostram personagem em meio a manifestantes e policiais na capital francesa. Fato ou Fake analisou o material com ferramentas de detecção de IA.
articles.body:
É #FAKE imagem de Pantera Cor-de-Rosa nos protestos em Paris; imagem foi criada com IA — Foto: Reprodução

Circulam nas redes sociais imagens que supostamente mostram uma pessoa fantasiada de Pantera Cor-de-Rosa durante os protestos em Paris , na França. É FAKE .

Publicadas no X, no Instagram e no Facebook, as imagens mostram uma pessoa fantasiada de Pantera Cor-de-Rosa em diferentes situações durante os protestos em Paris. Em uma delas, a personagem aparece saltando, com uma das mãos levantadas, enquanto é atingida na barriga por um cassetete. Em outra, está diante de um canhão de água. Há ainda uma cena em que aparece sendo carregada por policiais. Todas foram criadas com inteligência artificial (IA) .

Veja dois exemplos de legendas que acompanham o material: "A Pantera Cor-de-Rosa nos protestos da França, fala-me de aura"; e "A Pantera Cor-de-Rosa também participou nos protestos em França. Esse gesto de desafio contra o canhão de água é um tipo de resistência absurda e teatral que, de certa forma, faz com que imagens dos distúrbios pareçam uma performance. Esta imagem, que vale por mil palavras, mostra a dimensão simbólica e visual que estas manifestações também têm".

As imagens manipuladas circulam em meio a uma onda de protestos na França . As manifestações contra a inflação e cortes em serviços públicos deixaram um morto, mais de 500 policiais feridos e quase 1.800 pessoas detidas até sábado (17).

O Fato ou Fake submeteu o material a ferramentas que detectam conteúdos criados com inteligência artificial. Todas apontaram o uso dessa tecnologia (veja os resultados das análises e infográficos a seguir).

Pantera pulando e sendo atingida por cassetete:

SynthID Detector - "SynthID detectado. Este conteúdo foi criado ou editado com IA do Google." Essa tecnologia insere em fotos, vídeos e áudios uma marca d'água imperceptível para humanos (que não conseguem verificar o indicador apenas observando as cenas ou escutando os contéudos). Mas ela é detectável pelo sistema. Diferentemente de outros modelos que geram deepfakes a partir de materiais reais, a IA do Google produz materiais hiper-realistas do zero, ou seja, sem a referência de algo verdadeiro publicado anteriormente.

Hive Moderation - 99,9% de chances de ter sido criado com IA.

SightEngine - 99% de chances de ter sido criado com IA.

Sightegine aponta uso de IA em imagem de Pantera Cor-de-Rosa nos protestos em Paris — Foto: Reprodução

HiveModeration aponta uso de IA em imagem de Pantera Cor-de-Rosa em protestos em Paris — Foto: Reprodução

O Fato ou Fake submeteu a foto ao detector de inteligência artificial (IA) da OpenAI , dona do ChatGPT, que consegue identificar imagens criadas com modelos da própria empresa. Resultado da análise: "Gerado com ferramentas da OpenAI. Os sinais abaixo fornecem evidências que corroboram este resultado: SynthID detectado. Credenciais de conteúdo não detectadas " (veja o infográfico abaixo).

OpenAI Verify apontou que pantera rosa em frente a canhão foi criada com ferramentas da OpenAI. — Foto: Reprodução

SightEngine - 97% de chances de ter sido criado com IA.

Sightengine aponta uso de IA em imagem de Pantera Cor-de-Rosa em protestos em Paris — Foto: Reprodução

articles.title: Mamdani says feds have abdicated on AI, urges New Yorkers to push back | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Monday night that New Yorkers must resist the narrative that an AI takeover is inevitable and demand regulations that protect the public and put power back in their hands.
articles.body:
Two of New York’s sweethearts, Mayor Zohran Mamdani and activist and “Broad City” star Ilana Glazer, spoke about AI at Webster Hall in Manhattan on Monday night, with Glazer posing questions to the mayor about the future of AI in society.

Mamdani encouraged New Yorkers to resist the overwhelming feeling that AI is inevitably coming for their jobs, their kids’ minds, and their dignity, and to take back control instead.

His message came at a moment when the federal government is doing little to regulate AI, leaving cities to act on their own. At The People’s AI Assembly, an event hosted by the AI Now Institute , a think tank that explores the social implications of AI, Mamdani argued that the technology’s rapid rollout is not inevitable and that public officials should hold AI companies accountable.

Last month, Mamdani ordered a ban on AI use in elementary and middle schools. Glazer, a parent, said the technology’s arrival in classrooms unsettles her.

“It just makes me nervous. It feels so non-consensual, as though…this has to be in schools. It wasn’t two years ago. Why does it have to be in schools?” she said.

Over the summer, the mayor also introduced a policy that would require landlords, brokers, and real estate platforms to clearly disclose when a property’s listing photos or videos are made with AI. The policy is aimed at protecting New Yorkers from getting “house-phished,” or tricked by misleading listings.

Both moves challenge the assumption that schools and the public must simply accept AI as it arrives.

“Nothing has to be,” Mamdani said at the event Monday. “There’s a creep that comes with this, and there’s an intent to overwhelm that leaves people feeling as if there is simply no option.”

He said there has been a “reckless adoption of technology without any kind of a reckoning with the limitations of that technology,” citing the U.S. military’s February strike on a school in Iran that killed more than 150 people, including at least 123 children . Officials involved in the Pentagon’s internal investigation have told Bloomberg that overreliance on AI in targeting was one factor in the attack.

“There is this desire to speak about [AI] as if it is infallible, as if it cannot be questioned, as if the only people who can regulate it are the ones who are currently developing it,” Mamdani said, noting that Facebook made similar arguments back in 2008. “What it really is,’ he continued, “is an attempt to escape any kind of accountability at any level, without also jeopardizing the potential valuation from an IPO.”

Anthropic is expected to debut on the public markets this year, and OpenAI has said it will go public in 2027.

Mamdani criticized the “complete abdication of federal law” when it comes to AI.

“At a national level, when the conversation is about artificial intelligence, it’s so often framed in this language of an arms race with China, and any of the humanistic concern, we just push to the side in a language of national competition,” the mayor said.

President Donald Trump’s Superintelligence Task Force , announced earlier this month, largely focuses on allowing powerful AI companies to self-regulate, rather than creating new federal restrictions. That comes despite growing fears about AI’s effect on every facet of human life, including warnings from whistleblowers at Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and OpenAI that AI could lead to human extinction.

“As we are looking at what comes after this federal administration, there has to be a very different kind of framework in how we think about AI, talk about AI, the accountability we’re willing to bring forward when it comes to that,” Mamdani said.

articles.title: An AI bust could come from places investors aren't watching, an economist says
articles.summary: Concerns about an AI bubble are growing as investors question whether massive spending on chips and data centers will pay off.
articles.body:
Concerns about an AI bubble are growing as investors question whether massive capex spending will pay off.

TS Lombard warns that debt, a potential chip glut, and political backlash could threaten the AI trade.

Much of AI's revenue growth still comes from spending within the industry itself, TS Lombard economist says.

As concerns about an AI bubble mount, an economist is warning that investors may be overlooking other vulnerabilities in the boom.

"The trigger doesn't have to be endogenous to the boom. It could be external," wrote Dario Perkins, managing director of global macro at Global Data.TS Lombard, in a note on Monday.

Perkins argues that much of the industry's revenue growth still comes from spending within the AI ecosystem rather than businesses and consumers paying for AI services.

"The question is whether those revenues are coming from businesses and end-users outside the ecosystem — presumably to pay for productivity-enhancing tools — or from simple capex recycling," he wrote.

The warning comes after a recent chip-stocks selloff that has intensified concerns about whether massive AI infrastructure spending will pay off.

Last week, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell more than 11% before clawing back 2% on Monday.

One potential fault line is debt outside Big Tech.

While hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Amazon, and Google have strong balance sheets, smaller cloud providers, model developers, and infrastructure suppliers have been taking on increasing leverage.

Perkins estimates that debt across parts of the AI ecosystem could reach $2 trillion by the end of 2027.

He doesn't see AI-related debt as a systemic financial risk, but warned that earnings disappointments and canceled orders could ripple across the ecosystem. Even cash-rich hyperscalers could decide not to renew data center leases, leaving weaker companies exposed.

Another risk is an unexpected chip glut, as companies reportedly over-order semiconductors to guard against shortages, potentially creating excess supply if demand slows.

"Let's not forget we are talking about tech hardware and chips, notoriously cyclical, and prone to bullwhip effects," Perkins wrote.

Higher interest rates could further undermine the economics of AI investment, particularly for companies reliant on borrowing to finance their expansion.

But Perkins sees another potential trigger that has little to do with corporate earnings: political backlash.

"AI boosters on social media live in a bubble," Perkins wrote.

"They don't realize that ordinary people don't like AI. They don't find it useful, they REALLY don't want to live near datacenters, and they are worried about their jobs. And they vote," he added.

Perkins suggested that a single high-profile incident could rapidly turn that unease into broader opposition.

"One high-profile accident turns AI toxic," he wrote.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: Former OpenAI engineer denied bail over alleged recording device; Saudi Arabia offered $1 million guarantee
articles.summary: A federal judge in the US has ordered former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan to remain in jail after questioning whether a $1 million bond backed by
articles.body: A federal judge in the US has ordered former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan to remain in jail after questioning whether a $1 million bond backed by Saudi Arabia would ensure he returned to court if released. Alfozan, 35, was arrested on October 9 over allegations that he planted a recording device in an OpenAI conference room where executives and, at times, government officials discussed sensitive information. According to a Fortune report, he will remain in federal custody until his next court date on November 6. Alfozan faces a charge related to intercepting oral communications and has not been indicted or entered a plea.Why the judge rejected the $1 million bail offerMagistrate Judge Alex G. Tse questioned whether the proposed bond would be enough to prevent Alfozan from leaving the US. “Once he leaves, there’s no getting him back, and that’s why this is a bigger case,” Tse said in court.Alfozan’s lawyer, William Pernik, argued that his client planned to return to the US after accompanying his wife and young son to Saudi Arabia during paternity leave. The Saudi Consulate General in Los Angeles offered to cover the full amount of any bail bond set by the court. It also said it would not issue travel documents to Alfozan if he were released.What FBI allegedly found on his phoneCourt filings say investigators found electronic components at Alfozan’s home that were similar to the recording device allegedly placed behind a television in the conference room.The FBI also found photographs on his iPhone, dated September 22 to September 28, showing another recording device and television connections inside OpenAI buildings. Some images were taken in locations where sensitive meetings were held.US prosecutors said the photographs suggested Alfozan had looked for places where additional devices could be installed. His lawyer disputed the government’s account, saying the conference room was open to people who worked there.Prosecutors said they did not know what information Alfozan may have intended to take from OpenAI or the US.“That is the concern, that something is going to leave OpenAI and the U.S., and quite frankly we don’t even know what that is,” Assistant US Attorney Nick Parker said.What OpenAI and Alfozan’s lawyer have saidOpenAI ended Alfozan’s employment on October 9, according to the report. The company has said it has “no indications” that he improperly accessed or took model weights, source code or customer data. Alfozan’s defence stressed that the criminal complaint does not accuse him of espionage, stealing trade secrets or acting as an agent of a foreign government.His lawyer also said Alfozan had lived in the US for 15 years, obtained a green card in 2020 and intended to return to his job after paternity leave.You use AI every day. articles.title: The far left wants to kill the tech that can create Trump’s golden age
articles.summary: Bernie Sanders wants to nationalize 50% of the AI industry and jail scientists, while Trump and Elon Musk push for a technological golden age.
articles.body: America seems to be on the precipice of a future technological golden age. Whether we take steps toward that future could depend on which political vision prevails over the next few election cycles. Speaking alongside President Donald Trump at the White House in September, Elon Musk predicted a world where artificial intelligence and advanced robotics create an "age of abundance." Musk suggests these technologies could eventually provide your average person with better medical care than what today’s wealthiest individuals enjoy. TRUMP TO USHER IN ‘GOLDEN AGE’ OF AMERICAN TECH WITH DC BASH SHOWCASING POWERFUL NEW TOOL This optimistic vision aligns well with Trump’s repeated promises of a new American golden age. Yet, as his administration works to accelerate technological advancement, an increasingly influential wing on the far left appears determined to slam on the brakes. Trump’s vision of a golden age The Trump administration has made American leadership in artificial intelligence a cornerstone of its economic agenda. Through its AI Action Plan and executive orders, the administration has prioritized eliminating regulatory barriers, constructing data centers and expanding energy infrastructure necessary to power the AI revolution. TRUMP ANNOUNCES NEW 'AI FORCE,' VOWS TO PROTECT INDUSTRY AS AI CZAR ANNOUNCEMENT NEARS Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued that AI and automation could help create a new era of American manufacturing. In an interview from 2025, Bessent suggested that the advanced "smart factories" of tomorrow could overcome labor-cost issues, making manufacturing in the United States far more economically feasible. Imagine a future in America where advanced robotics makes domestic manufacturing globally competitive, where AI leads to major medical breakthroughs and where technological innovation produces unprecedented economic prosperity. THE NEXT AMERICAN BOOM COULD BE HERE — UNLESS WASHINGTON REGULATES IT TO DEATH Of course, there are legitimate questions about how this societal transformation will unfold, but the potential benefits are incredible. The far left wants to hit the brakes While many in the Trump administration plan for a golden age, Vermont Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders and his fellow democratic socialists are promoting an entirely different future. In March, Sanders and New York Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez proposed a nationwide moratorium on new data center construction until Congress establishes a sufficient regulatory system for the industry. INSIDE THE FAR-LEFT'S ANTI-DATA CENTER PUSH AND WHAT EXPERTS SAY IS DRIVING IT: 'PLAYBOOK WE'VE SEEN BEFORE' These positions have quickly become commonplace for Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) activists and candidates. Many of these DSA-endorsed candidates support data center moratoriums and push these sorts of proposals at the state and local level. But Sanders’ anti-AI sentiment goes way further. His American AI Sovereign Wealth Fund Act would effectively nationalize 50% of the AI industry, converting those stakes into a government-controlled fund. The plan would also include stacking the boards of these companies with federally picked appointees to influence corporate decisions. SANDERS PUSHES 'DEATH PENALTY' FOR CRUCIAL US INDUSTRY THAT COULD GIVE ADVANTAGE TO FOREIGN ADVERSARIES More recently, Sanders introduced legislation that would permanently prohibit the development of artificial superintelligence. This plan would establish a new federal AI agency and halt other advanced AI development until regulators approve continued efforts. Under this proposal, individuals who violate the research bans could face up to 20 years in federal prison. The Trump administration has made American leadership in artificial intelligence a cornerstone of its economic agenda. Think about that. At a time when America is competing with China for technological supremacy, one of the country’s most prominent socialist politicians wants federal bureaucrats to target AI scientists with potential prison time for developing AI research it deems too advanced. WINNING THE AI RACE MEANS BEATING CHINA ON INNOVATION, COST AND TRUST The cost of standing still To be sure, the AI revolution comes with many legitimate concerns that deserve conversation. Potential job displacement, privacy violations, algorithmic manipulation and the possible misuse of advanced AI are issues that will likely need to be addressed. However, the consequences of deliberately suppressing technological innovation are rarely given equal attention. Consider the potential benefits of AI-assisted drug discovery, which could lead to better treatments for cancer, Alzheimer’s and many other conditions. AI-enhanced robotics and logistics could transform manufacturing, increase agricultural output and help elderly and disabled Americans maintain their independence. Imagine the lives and the industries that could be saved and the economic opportunities that could spring up from these technologies that we have only now begun to understand. Under the far left’s proposals, we may never see these benefits materialize. Sanders says he is concerned that average Americans will be left behind in the AI revolution, but his proposed restrictions threaten to undermine the very innovations that could cause growth in societal prosperity. China won’t be hitting the brakes Perhaps the most concerning consequence of the far left’s vision is America’s geopolitical future. Like America, China is also pursuing AI at breakneck speeds. While America has enjoyed a substantial lead in this race, the recent Stanford University 2026 AI Index showed the performance gap between American and Chinese models has effectively disappeared. The proposals from Sanders and the far left to stall AI research and data center construction give the Chinese Communist Party opportunity to pull ahead in the AI race. If China were to take the lead in the AI race, America’s global status economically and geopolitically could be severely diminished. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION At the same White House meeting where Musk outlined his optimistic vision of the future, Trump warned that Chinese President Xi Jinping "will take every data center that we don’t want." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The AI revolution carries great potential for increased prosperity unlike anything we have seen in our lifetime. It would be a historic tragedy if America surrendered that opportunity because our politicians were more afraid of technological progress than our geopolitical rivals.

articles.title: Sam Altman to employees, we can save the world from ‘dangerous AI’, but we cannot do it alone; need …
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has told employees that preventing advanced AI from becoming dangerous will require cooperation beyond a single company.
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has told employees that preventing advanced AI from becoming dangerous will require cooperation beyond a single company. According to a report by The Information, Sam Altman outlined three possible approaches to AI safety, including setting up an international body similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), bringing major AI labs together under one organisation, or allowing one company to gain enough power to stop other developers from building dangerous systems. As quoted in the report, Altman said he opposed the third option. His comments come as concerns grow over AI safety and the US government considers stronger oversight of leading AI developers.Sam Altman outlines 3 plans to make AI saferThe report cites people familiar with the discussion saying that Altman described three possible paths for the industry.An international AI watchdog: A global organisation similar to the IAEA could set safety standards and oversee advanced AI development. This approach would require cooperation between countries developing leading AI models, including the US and China.A single AI research body: Major AI companies could combine their work through one organisation, similar to CERN, the international particle physics research centre. The body could develop AI models for countries working with it.One company controls AI development: A single developer could gain enough economic power to restrict other companies' access to computing resources, preventing them from developing potentially dangerous systems.Sam Altman reportedly called the third approach the “Eliezer plan”, referring to AI safety researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky. “Obviously I think that one’s terrible,” Altman said.Why OpenAI is discussing AI safety nowThe discussion comes amid concerns that advanced AI systems could be misused for cyberattacks or act in ways their developers did not intend. The report said AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta had recently been involved in breaches of company systems.OpenAI has also faced internal questions about its commitment to safety after firing three researchers focused on the issue, according to the report. Sam Altman has said there are too few workable proposals for slowing AI development and that humans must remain in control of the technology.US considers stronger checks on AI companiesThe Trump administration has so far focused on voluntary agreements that allow it to review new AI models before public release. However, Pentagon official Emil Michael has indicated that stricter checks could be considered if AI companies put people or businesses at risk.OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are also working on a proposed US group called the Standards Authority for Frontier AI. It could support independent evaluators and establish ways for companies to report safety and security incidents.However, the companies have yet to agree on who should test new models.Altman said OpenAI could not afford to fall behind its competitors, even as the industry considers ways to make AI development safer. He told employees that the company would need to decide which approach to support over the next year.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
